profile.feeling: A first day at school, a first visit, the winner of a race.

examples.tr: It’s my first day at work.
It’s my first time in Israel.
She arrived first.

phrases.tr: I am the first and I am the last
phrases.meaning: the eternal one, before and after everything

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym for the ordinal; the adverb “first, at first” is another word (קֹדֶם, בְּהַתְחָלָה).

etymology.text: From the root ר־א־שׁ of רֹאשׁ “head”, in the pattern קִטְלוֹן (Wiktionary): “the one at the head”.

funFacts: Sunday is יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן, “the first day” of the week.
pitfalls: The א is silent: rishón.
It agrees like any adjective: הַפַּעַם הָרִאשׁוֹנָה, הַיָּמִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים — and the article is הָ before ר.
subtleties: After a verb it says who came first and agrees with the subject: הִיא הִגִּיעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה, הֵם הִגִּיעוּ רִאשׁוֹנִים.

profile.feeling: Second place, a second chance, a second-hand car.

examples.tr: We live in the second house on the left.
This is the second time I’m here.
We bought a second-hand car.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym for the ordinal; the adverb “secondly, again” is שֵׁנִית.

etymology.text: From the number שְׁנַיִם “two” (Proto-Semitic *ṯin-, Wiktionary) with the ending ־ִי.

funFacts: Monday is יוֹם שֵׁנִי, “the second day”.
pitfalls: שְׁנִיָּה is also a noun, “a second” (of time): חַכֵּה שְׁנִיָּה! “wait a second!”.
שֵׁנִי “second” ≠ שְׁנֵי “two (of)”: שְׁנֵי בָּתִּים “two houses”, הַבַּיִת הַשֵּׁנִי “the second house”.
The feminine doubles the י: שְׁנִיָּה (full spelling שנייה).
subtleties: Wiktionary also gives the feminine שֵׁנִית; today שֵׁנִית is mainly the adverb “again, secondly”.

profile.feeling: The third floor without a lift; a third child.

examples.tr: They live on the third floor.
This is their third child.
She finished in third place.

etymology.text: From שָׁלוֹשׁ “three” (root שׁ־ל־שׁ) in the ordinal pattern קְטִילִי, like רְבִיעִי, חֲמִישִׁי, שְׁבִיעִי (Wiktionary gives no etymology).

funFacts: Tuesday, יוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי, is a favourite day for weddings: in Genesis “it was good” is said twice on the third day.
pitfalls: A third (⅓) is the noun שְׁלִישׁ, plural שְׁלִישִׁים — and Wiktionary also lists שְׁלִישִׁים as a plural of the ordinal; the usual plural of “third” is שְׁלִישִׁיִּים.
subtleties: The ordinal pattern קְטִילִי: שְׁלִישִׁי, רְבִיעִי, חֲמִישִׁי, שְׁבִיעִי, שְׁמִינִי, תְּשִׁיעִי, עֲשִׂירִי — first, second and sixth are irregular.

profile.feeling: Just off the podium: the fourth place.

examples.tr: This is our fourth trip this year.
She lives on the fourth floor.
He finished fourth.

etymology.text: From אַרְבַּע “four” (root ר־ב־ע) in the ordinal pattern קְטִילִי (Wiktionary gives no etymology).

funFacts: Wednesday is יוֹם רְבִיעִי, “the fourth day”.
pitfalls: The article before ר is הָ: הָרְבִיעִי, הָרְבִיעִית.
A quarter is רֶבַע (lesson C04), not רְבִיעִי; a quartet is a רְבִיעִיָּה.
subtleties: The א of אַרְבַּע is not part of the root: four is ר־ב־ע, as in רֶבַע and רְבִיעִי.

profile.feeling: Thursday evening, the fifth lesson of a long school day.

examples.tr: The fifth lesson starts at one.
We live in the fifth house in the street.
Their fifth daughter was born in May.

etymology.text: From חָמֵשׁ “five” (Wiktionary), in the ordinal pattern קְטִילִי.

funFacts: Thursday is יוֹם חֲמִישִׁי, “the fifth day”.
pitfalls: Wiktionary also lists the short plural חֲמִישִׁים — in everyday spelling the same letters as חֲמִשִּׁים “fifty” (חמישים); the plural in use is חֲמִישִׁיִּים.
The article before ח is הַ without a dagesh: הַחֲמִישִׁי.
subtleties: The fifth of something (⅕) is חֲמִישִׁית, the same as the feminine ordinal.

examples.tr: She has a sixth sense.
The office is on the sixth floor.
This is his sixth book.

etymology.text: From שֵׁשׁ “six”; Wiktionary gives no etymology. Unlike the other ordinals from three to ten it has a doubled שׁ, not the pattern קְטִילִי.

funFacts: Friday is יוֹם שִׁשִּׁי — Israelis often just say שִׁשִּׁי.
pitfalls: Full spelling שישי (Wiktionary marks ששי as defective).
Wiktionary lists two masculine plurals; שִׁשִּׁים is also “sixty” — the plural of the ordinal in use is שִׁשִּׁיִּים.
subtleties: The feminine שִׁשִּׁית is also “a sixth” (⅙).

profile.feeling: The day of rest; seventh heaven.

examples.tr: The Sabbath is the seventh day.

examples.text: הַחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי שֶׁל הַשָּׁנָה הוּא יוּלִי.
examples.tr: The seventh month of the year is July.
He was in seventh heaven.

etymology.text: From שֶׁבַע “seven” (root שׁ־ב־ע) in the ordinal pattern קְטִילִי (Wiktionary gives no etymology).

funFacts: The week, שָׁבוּעַ, has the same root: a unit of seven days.
pitfalls: Wiktionary also lists the short plural שְׁבִיעִים — in everyday spelling close to שִׁבְעִים “seventy” (שבעים); the plural in use is שְׁבִיעִיִּים.
subtleties: In Hebrew the seventh day of the week is Saturday, the Sabbath — the week starts on Sunday.

profile.feeling: A high floor, an old ritual on the eighth day.

examples.tr: He lives on the eighth floor.
The circumcision is on the eighth day.
This is the eighth chapter of the book.

etymology.text: From שְׁמוֹנֶה “eight” (Proto-Semitic *ṯamāniy-, Wiktionary) in the ordinal pattern קְטִילִי.

funFacts: The festival after Sukkot is שְׁמִינִי עֲצֶרֶת, “the eighth (day) of assembly”.
pitfalls: Not שְׁמוֹנִים “eighty”: the plural of the ordinal is שְׁמִינִיִּים.
subtleties: The feminine שְׁמִינִית is also “an eighth” (⅛).

profile.feeling: September, the ninth month; the last year of middle school.

examples.tr: The ninth month is September.
He is in ninth grade.
It’s her ninth year in the company.

etymology.text: From תֵּשַׁע “nine” (root ת־שׁ־ע) in the ordinal pattern קְטִילִי (Wiktionary gives no etymology).

funFacts: School grades are written with letters: ninth grade is כִּתָּה ט׳ (ט = 9).
pitfalls: Not תִּשְׁעִים “ninety”: the plural of the ordinal is תְּשִׁיעִיִּים.
subtleties: The feminine תְּשִׁיעִית is also “a ninth” (1⁄9).

profile.feeling: The last ordinal — after ten Hebrew counts with ordinary numbers.

examples.tr: It’s the tenth day of the trip.

examples.text: אֲנִי אוֹמֵר לְךָ אֶת זֶה בַּפַּעַם הָעֲשִׂירִית!
examples.tr: I’m telling you this for the tenth time!
Her office is on the tenth floor.

etymology.text: From עֶשֶׂר “ten” (root ע־שׂ־ר) in the ordinal pattern קְטִילִי (Wiktionary gives no etymology).

funFacts: The tithe, מַעֲשֵׂר, “the tenth part”, has the same root.
pitfalls: The last ordinal: from 11 on the cardinal with the article follows the noun — הַיּוֹם הָאַחַד עָשָׂר “the eleventh day”, הַקּוֹמָה הָעֶשְׂרִים “the twentieth floor”.
The article before ע is הָ: הָעֲשִׂירִי.
subtleties: The feminine עֲשִׂירִית is also “a tenth” (0.1).

governs.none: takes no complement of its own

lexemes.note: Last (and latest). An adjective like the ordinals: הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס הָאַחֲרוֹן, הַפַּעַם הָאַחֲרוֹנָה.

profile.feeling: The last bus of the night, the last page, the latest news.

examples.tr: This is the last bus tonight.

examples.text: בַּפַּעַם הָאַחֲרוֹנָה שֶׁרָאִיתִי אוֹתוֹ, הוּא הָיָה יֶלֶד.
examples.tr: The last time I saw him, he was a child.
He arrived last.
Have you heard the latest news?

synonyms.nuance: “final” — a result, a decision, an answer

etymology.text: From the root א־ח־ר “after, behind” (as in אַחֲרֵי) in the pattern קִטְלוֹן (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Isaiah 44:6: אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן וַאֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן “I am the first and I am the last”.
pitfalls: “Last week” is בַּשָּׁבוּעַ שֶׁעָבַר; הַשָּׁבוּעַ הָאַחֲרוֹן is “the past seven days” or “the final week”.
The article before א is הָ: הָאַחֲרוֹן, הָאַחֲרוֹנָה.
subtleties: With news and time it means “latest”: הַחֲדָשׁוֹת הָאַחֲרוֹנוֹת, בַּזְּמַן הָאַחֲרוֹן.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

meaningForms.note: only the construct before a measure: חֲצִי קִילוֹ, חֲצִי שָׁעָה
after a number, with the older absolute form חֵצִי: שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי “three and a half; half past three”

lexemes.note: Half. Before a noun it is the construct חֲצִי (חֲצִי שָׁעָה); after a number וָחֵצִי (שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי).

profile.feeling: Half a sandwich, half an hour of waiting, half price in the sales.

senses.def: half (a part of something: חֲצִי מֵהָעוּגָה)
half a … (before a measure: חֲצִי קִילוֹ, חֲצִי שָׁעָה)

examples.tr: I ate only half.
Half of the pupils didn’t come.
I waited half an hour.
I bought half a kilo of tomatoes.

synonyms.nuance: “half” in writing and statistics: מַחֲצִית הַשָּׁנָה (Wiktionary lists it as a synonym)
“half” in set phrases: עַל מֶחֱצָה “by half” (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From the root ח־צ־ה “to split in two” (as in חָצָה “to cross; to halve”), pattern קֵטֶל (Wiktionary). Wiktionary gives both forms, חֲצִי and the older absolute חֵצִי.

funFacts: The same root gives חֲצוֹת “midnight” — the night cut in half.
pitfalls: No word for “a / an”: חֲצִי שָׁעָה “half an hour”, חֲצִי קִילוֹ “half a kilo”.
After a number the form is חֵצִי with וָ: שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי “three and a half”, also on the clock “half past three”.
subtleties: Wiktionary gives the gender as masculine or feminine; in use it is mostly masculine: הַחֲצִי הַשֵּׁנִי “the second half”.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A quarter. רֶבַע שָׁעָה “a quarter of an hour”; on the clock רֶבַע לְ… / … וָרֶבַע.

override.N;PL;INDF: Wiktionary’s head line vowels the plural רְבַעִים (patach); a segolate like רֶבַע has qamats in the plural, as רֶגַע → רְגָעִים and זֶרַע → זְרָעִים: רְבָעִים.

profile.feeling: The clock face divided in four; a quarter of a cake.

senses.def: a quarter, one fourth (also of an hour)

examples.tr: It’s a quarter to three.
We waited a quarter of an hour.
Let’s meet at a quarter past three.
He ate a quarter of the cake.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in everyday use; a quarter of a town is another word, רֹבַע (Wiktionary).

etymology.text: From the root ר־ב־ע “four” (as in אַרְבַּע, רְבִיעִי) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The four quarters of the Old City of Jerusalem are each a רֹבַע — with o, a different word.
pitfalls: רֶבַע “a quarter” ≠ רֹבַע “a quarter (district) of a town” ≠ רְבִיעִי “fourth”.
On the clock: … וָרֶבַע “a quarter past …”, רֶבַע לְ… “a quarter to …”, with the feminine numbers of the hours: רֶבַע לְאַרְבַּע.
subtleties: Three quarters: שְׁלוֹשָׁה רְבָעִים — רֶבַע is masculine.

pattern.none: a primary word, not a pattern

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A century — the noun of the number מֵאָה (lesson 5). Feminine: הַמֵּאָה הָעֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת.

profile.feeling: History lessons, old buildings, “the last century”.

examples.tr: We live in the twenty-first century.
The house was built in the last century.
It happened in the first century AD.

profile.synonymsNone: No other word for a century.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *miʾat- (Wiktionary) — the same word as the number מֵאָה “a hundred”: a hundred years.

funFacts: Hebrew counts centuries with the hundred itself: “the twentieth hundred” = the twentieth century.
pitfalls: The same word is the number 100: מֵאָה שָׁנִים “a hundred years” — but הַמֵּאָה הָעֶשְׂרִים “the twentieth century”. The article and the number after it show the century.
Feminine, so the number after it is feminine: הַמֵּאָה הָעֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת, הַמֵּאָה הַשְּׁמוֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה; centuries 1–10 take the feminine ordinal: הַמֵּאָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה.
subtleties: Years and centuries are often counted לַסְּפִירָה “of the (common) era” and לִפְנֵי הַסְּפִירָה “before the era”.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A decade. Article הֶעָשׂוֹר, with בְּ: בֶּעָשׂוֹר.

profile.feeling: Ten years gone: anniversaries, reunions, the news looking back.

examples.tr: In the last decade the city has grown a lot.
A decade has passed since then.
They have been married for a decade.

synonyms.nuance: “ten years” — the everyday way to say it

etymology.text: From the root ע־שׂ־ר “ten”, pattern קָטוֹל (Wiktionary, whose senses are “a period of ten days” and “a decade, a period of ten years”).

funFacts: In the Bible עָשׂוֹר is the tenth day of a month: Yom Kippur falls בֶּעָשׂוֹר לַחֹדֶשׁ, “on the tenth of the month” (Leviticus 16:29).
pitfalls: The article before the unstressed עָ is הֶ: הֶעָשׂוֹר, and with בְּ: בֶּעָשׂוֹר.
In speech עֶשֶׂר שָׁנִים is more common; עָשׂוֹר sounds a little formal.
subtleties: Wiktionary’s first sense is the older “ten days” — the modern meaning is a decade.

root.none: a compound of two words (יוֹם + הַשָּׁנָה): each part has its own root

pattern.none: a compound of two words, not one pattern

plurals.none: no plural in use (יְמֵי הַשָּׁנָה means “the days of the year”)

construct.none: a compound that already contains the article: it is not put into the construct (“the anniversary of …” is יוֹם הַשָּׁנָה לְ…)

lexemes.note: An anniversary. A compound with the article inside: יוֹם הַשָּׁנָה לְ… “the anniversary of …”.

profile.feeling: Flowers on a wedding anniversary; a memorial ceremony on the same date each year.

senses.def: an anniversary (of an event, a death, a wedding)

examples.tr: Today is our anniversary.

examples.text: בְּיוֹם הַשָּׁנָה לַחֲתֻנָּה הוּא קָנָה לָהּ פְּרָחִים.
examples.tr: On their wedding anniversary he bought her flowers.
The anniversary ceremony will be tomorrow.

synonyms.nuance: “a wedding anniversary” — only of a marriage
“a jubilee” — a fiftieth (or a big round) anniversary (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: יוֹם “day” + הַשָּׁנָה “the year”: “the day of the year”. Wiktionary has no entry for the compound; its parts are checked under יוֹם and שָׁנָה.

funFacts: For a death the yearly memorial is the same expression; the ceremony at the grave is an אַזְכָּרָה.
pitfalls: The article is already inside: “our anniversary” = יוֹם הַשָּׁנָה שֶׁלָּנוּ; “the anniversary of …” = יוֹם הַשָּׁנָה לְ… (with לְ, not שֶׁל).
subtleties: A couple’s anniversary is just as often יוֹם הַנִּשּׂוּאִין שֶׁלָּנוּ.
